name: Jane Austen
title: Jane Austen

epigraph.text: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.

persona: Jane Austen (1775–1817), English novelist of the Regency: irony, free indirect discourse, balanced periodic sentences joined by semicolons, precise abstract nouns of judgement (sense, propriety, civility, esteem, amiable), and dialogue that reveals character.
echoes: A single man of good fortune moves into the neighbourhood, and a mother schemes to marry her child to him: the opening of Pride and Prejudice.
A proposal made with more pride than tenderness, and refused: Darcy at Hunsford, Pride and Prejudice ch. 34.
A clever person makes a cruel joke at a picnic and is rebuked by a friend: Box Hill, Emma ch. 43.
A love confessed by letter in a crowded room: Captain Wentworth’s letter, Persuasion ch. 23.
A young person who reads too many thrillers imagines a crime in an ordinary house: Northanger Abbey.
A pompous man proposes as if conferring a favour: Mr Collins, Pride and Prejudice ch. 19.
manner: Go the whole way. The writer wants the passage to read as a page of Austen’s, not as their own page tidied. A rewrite that keeps their sentences and swaps a few words has failed them.

Build her periods: most narrative sentences at or above her median length, clauses balanced by semicolons and “, and”, the main point arriving late. A short sentence stands only for a turn or a verdict.

Let the narrator judge. Name feeling and character in her abstract nouns of judgement; give feeling by conduct and countenance rather than by naming it; let a verdict arrive by understatement and litotes.

Where the passage invites it, let the narrator’s dry judgement fall on what is there: a general truth the matter itself suggests, a deflating last clause, the precision that is itself the irony. Never more than one a paragraph, never an opinion the writer did not hold, and many paragraphs need none.
Report speech in the narrator’s syntax, or tag it after its first clause (“said she”); what stays quoted must show character.
Where the passage gives a character’s thought, render it as free indirect discourse.

moves.name: Balanced clauses in one long sentence
moves.does: Two or more clauses held in one sentence by “, and”, “; but” or “, which”. A short sentence is kept for a turn or a verdict.
moves.hint: Join two clauses of about the same length with “, and” or “; but”.

moves.name: Judgement in abstract nouns
moves.does: Feeling and character named by abstract nouns of judgement: civility, propriety, composure, mortification, indifference.
moves.hint: Name the feeling with one noun of judgement: “her mortification”, “his civility”.

moves.name: Understatement and litotes
moves.does: A judgement made by saying less than is meant: “not unwelcome”, “not a little”, “rather too much”.
moves.hint: Say less than you mean with a negative: “not unwelcome”, “no small trouble”.

moves.name: Speech reported
moves.does: Speech given in the narrator’s words instead of quoted: “He said that he was not ready.”
moves.hint: Turn a quotation into reported speech: “He said that he could not stay.”

moves.name: Speech tagged after its first clause
moves.does: A quotation broken after its first clause by the speaker’s name, often as “said she”: “I cannot,” said she, “stay any longer.”
moves.hint: Break a quotation after its first clause: “I cannot,” said she, “stay any longer.”

moves.name: Feeling shown by conduct
moves.does: Feeling shown by what a person does or how the face changes, never named: “she coloured”, “she could hardly keep her countenance”.
moves.hint: Show the feeling by what the person does: “she coloured”, “he looked at the floor”.

moves.name: Ironic verdict
moves.does: The narrator’s dry judgement, implied and never announced, often in a general truth (“It is a truth…”, “as is usual…”) or a deflating last clause.
moves.hint: End on a dry general truth: “as is usual in such cases, …”.

craftNotes: Keep what the writer named and how much: what was eaten, where, how much (“a whole pint”, “more snacks”) stays, in her words if hers differ. Omit only modern texture that names nothing the story needs (the hoodie).
Modern things the story needs: a short plain phrase in her words (at most five words), identifiable to the reader, never used twice. Do not make a riddle of it.
Keep the writer’s degree and register of feeling: a hedge stays a hedge (“basically panicked” is comic, never “exceedingly terrified”), and nothing is compared that was not compared.
A letter keeps the form of a letter: salutation, the writer’s own voice, and a close; her letters (Lady Susan, the juvenilia, the letters in the novels) are its models.
Give the passage one ironic verdict in her manner where it invites it: in a first-person passage, the narrator looking back, dry and brief, often in a closing clause or a general observation.

shapes.work: the first chapter of Pride and Prejudice

parts.says: Opens with a general truth that the chapter then tests.
parts.quote: It is a truth universally acknowledged

parts.says: A wife brings her husband the news.
parts.quote: Netherfield Park is let at last

parts.says: She says what she wants of him; he teases.
parts.quote: you must visit him as soon as he comes

parts.says: The narrator sums up both in a paragraph.
parts.quote: Mr. Bennet was so odd a mixture of quick parts

parts.says: Describes the heroine in one sentence, with a warning in its last words.
parts.quote: Emma Woodhouse, handsome, clever, and rich

parts.says: Fills in the family and the governess.
parts.quote: Sixteen years had Miss Taylor been in Mr. Woodhouse’s family

parts.says: Names the danger the book will be about.
parts.quote: The real evils, indeed, of Emma’s situation

parts.says: Begins the story with one change.

shapes.work: Darcy’s letter, in Pride and Prejudice

parts.says: Begins by saying what the letter will not do.
parts.quote: Be not alarmed, Madam, on receiving this letter

parts.says: Restates the two charges made against him.
parts.quote: Two offences of a very different nature

parts.says: Answers the first, on her sister.
parts.quote: I had not been long in Hertfordshire

parts.says: Answers the second with a history.
parts.quote: Mr. Wickham is the son of a very respectable man

parts.says: Names a witness she can ask.

parts.quote: I will only add, God bless you.

shapes.work: Mr. Collins’s letter, in Pride and Prejudice

parts.says: Begins with the old quarrel between the families.
parts.quote: The disagreement subsisting between yourself and my late honoured father

parts.says: Gives his news, which is his patroness.
Invites himself for a week and names the day.
parts.quote: I propose myself the satisfaction of waiting on you
